roles.title: AI Product Manager
roles.reality: Owns a product whose core behaviour is probabilistic. Most of the job is deciding what the model should never do, defining acceptance criteria when outputs vary run to run, building evaluation sets, and negotiating the trade-off between autonomy and human review. Far more time goes into evals, guardrails and data access than into prompt wording.
screensFor: Can you write an evaluation set, and say what score would make you ship or stop?
Do you know when an LLM is the wrong tool (arithmetic, exact facts, regulated advice)?
Can you choose a level of automation that matches the cost of being wrong?
Do you understand retrieval, tool calling and routing well enough to scope them?
Can you cost a feature: tokens, latency, and what it does to unit economics?
evidenceThatCounts: A shipped AI feature with a written evaluation set and the results
A spec with explicit non-goals and a fail-closed design for the risky path
Evidence of a feature you killed or simplified because measurement said so
A human-in-the-loop review queue you designed, with its throughput cost
commonGaps: No evaluation discipline: demos instead of measured behaviour
Treats prompt tweaking as the product
Cannot reason about failure modes, hallucination and prompt injection
No view on cost per request or latency budgets
signals: Built with LLM APIs, retrieval or agent frameworks
Wrote specs, decision logs or PRDs
Evidence of measurement: funnels, A/B tests, eval sets, backtests
roles.demandNote: Every company with a model in production needs someone who can decide what it must never do. The supply of PMs who can write an eval set is far below demand, and the gap is widening rather than closing.

roles.title: Forward Deployed Engineer
roles.reality: Sits with the customer and builds the thing that makes the platform work in their messy reality: their data shapes, their auth, their compliance officer, their legacy export. Ships days-to-weeks increments in the customer's environment, then feeds recurring patterns back into the core product. Half engineering, half consulting; the deliverable is a working outcome, not a ticket closed.
screensFor: Can you build end to end alone: data in, UI out, deployed?
Can you sit in front of a frustrated customer and still make progress?
Do you scope ruthlessly and ship something usable this week?
Can you work with dirty, undocumented data and inconsistent APIs?
Do you know when to harden a prototype versus rebuild it?
evidenceThatCounts: Products you took from zero to running in someone else's environment
Integrations against ugly third-party data (exports, portals, legacy formats)
Evidence of customer contact: discovery notes, demos, support you handled
Fast, visible iteration history: small commits, frequent releases
commonGaps: Over-engineering when the job wanted a working demo on Friday
No deployment or operations story: it only ever ran locally
Weak written communication, which is most of the job
signals: Full-stack breadth: data pipeline, backend, frontend, deploy
Worked directly with clients, users or a first cohort
Evidence of integration work against external systems and APIs
roles.demandNote: The fastest-growing title in enterprise AI, and the hardest to fill: it wants an engineer who is willing to sit with a customer, which most strong engineers are not.

roles.title: Founding Engineer
roles.reality: Builds most of the product surface early, chooses the stack, and owns whatever is on fire. Judged on shipping speed with acceptable correctness, and on whether the choices made in month one are still liveable in year two.
screensFor: Breadth: can you own database, backend, frontend and deploys?
Judgement about what to build properly and what to fake for now
Comfort with ambiguity and direct user contact
Security and data correctness instincts under time pressure
evidenceThatCounts: A production system you designed and still operate
Payments, auth or other high-consequence flows built safely
A decision log showing trade-offs you made deliberately
commonGaps: No testing or delivery discipline once others must work in the code
Never operated anything with real users and real incidents
roles.demandNote: Constant demand at seed stage, but compensation is mostly equity and the failure rate is high. High leverage, high variance.

roles.title: AI Engineer
roles.reality: Builds the application layer over foundation models: retrieval, tool calling, routing, guardrails, evaluation harnesses and the plumbing that keeps them fast and affordable. Not model training; this is systems engineering where one component is stochastic.
screensFor: Retrieval design: chunking, embeddings, thresholds and citations
Tool/function calling and when to let code compute instead of the model
Evaluation harnesses and regression testing of prompts
Latency, cost and caching discipline
evidenceThatCounts: A repository with a real retrieval or agent pipeline and its eval set
Measured before/after numbers on quality, latency or cost
Guardrail design: input filtering, output checks, fail-closed routing
roles.demandNote: Demand is high but the field is crowding quickly with people who have shipped a demo. Evals, cost and guardrails are what still separate candidates.

roles.title: Solutions Architect (Cloud)
roles.reality: Designs how a customer's workload should run on a platform, and proves it: reference architectures, proofs of concept, cost models, migration plans. Success is measured in landed workloads, not diagrams.
screensFor: Reference architectures with cost and reliability trade-offs stated
Certification-level fluency in at least one major cloud
Ability to present to both engineers and finance
FinOps literacy: unit costs, commitments, waste
evidenceThatCounts: A documented architecture with a cost model behind it
Cloud certifications at associate level or above
A migration or cost-reduction you can quantify
roles.demandNote: Steady demand, and rising again as enterprises try to land AI workloads. Certifications carry unusual weight here compared with other engineering roles.

roles.title: Fintech Product Manager
roles.reality: Builds products where mistakes are money and regulators are stakeholders. The craft is designing flows that stay correct under partial failure, and writing the rules the product may not break.
screensFor: Do you understand settlement, reconciliation and idempotency?
Can you read the regulation that constrains the feature?
Can you design for auditability, not just happy paths?
evidenceThatCounts: A payment or investing flow you designed, including its failure handling
A compliance constraint you turned into a product decision
Domain certification (for example NISM in India, or equivalent)
commonGaps: Consumer-app instincts applied to regulated money
roles.demandNote: Solid and well paid, but the market is regional and regulated — the domain knowledge does not transfer across countries as cleanly as engineering does.

roles.title: Growth Engineer / Product Growth
roles.reality: Owns the funnel as a system: instrumentation, activation, retention loops and experiments. Builds the measurement before the campaign, and kills ideas that do not move a defined metric.
screensFor: Can you define activation and prove it predicts retention?
Do you know when your sample is too small for an A/B test?
Can you instrument a funnel and read a cohort chart?
evidenceThatCounts: A funnel you diagnosed with numbers before and after
A tracking plan you wrote and shipped
Experiments with pre-registered metrics, including the failures
signals: SEO or content systems with measured outcomes
roles.demandNote: Was extremely hot, has cooled. Still valued where the funnel is the business, but more competitive than it was.

roles.title: Platform / FinOps Engineer
roles.reality: Owns what the platform costs and whether it stays up. Tagging, unit costs, commitments and waste on one side; reliability, deploys and incident response on the other.
screensFor: Can you attribute cost to product surfaces and compute unit cost?
Do you know where money leaks: egress, idle, logging, over-provisioning?
Can you run a deploy pipeline and an incident?
evidenceThatCounts: A cost teardown with before/after numbers
Scale-to-zero or commitment decisions you made and measured
FinOps or cloud certification
commonGaps: Cost work without reliability experience, or the reverse
roles.demandNote: Cloud bills are under real scrutiny and few engineers can attribute cost to product surfaces. A small field with persistent openings.

roles.title: Founder / Technical Co-founder
roles.reality: Chooses the problem, finds the customers and builds enough product to earn the next month. The scarce skill is distribution and focus, not building.
screensFor: Evidence of customer discovery before building
A single market chosen deliberately
Honest unit economics, including acquisition cost
evidenceThatCounts: Paying customers, retention, or a channel with measured conversion
A funnel and its numbers
Written decision and kill criteria
roles.demandNote: Not a role anyone hires you into, and the expected value is dominated by a small number of outcomes. Listed for completeness, not as a career move.

roles.title: Technical Program Manager
roles.reality: Owns delivery across teams that do not report to you. Most of the job is making dependencies visible, forcing decisions that are being avoided, and keeping a launch honest about its date. Influence without authority is the whole craft, and the artefact is a plan other people actually follow.
screensFor: Can you run a programme across three teams with conflicting priorities?
Do you surface risk early, or report green until the week it slips?
Can you read an architecture well enough to challenge an estimate?
Do you drive decisions to closure, or just take notes?
evidenceThatCounts: A multi-team launch you coordinated, with the dependency map
A slip you called early, and what you changed because of it
Written status that a senior leader could act on without a meeting
commonGaps: Project administration mistaken for programme management
No technical depth, so estimates cannot be challenged
Reports status instead of removing blockers
roles.demandNote: Every company shipping AI features has more coordination load than it has people who can carry it. Steady demand, and one of the few senior roles reachable without writing production code.

roles.title: Product Manager
roles.reality: Decides what gets built and, more importantly, what does not. The output is not a roadmap but a sequence of decisions each backed by a reason someone can argue with. Most of the week is discovery, writing, and saying no to work that would not move the metric you own.
screensFor: Can you name the one metric this product moves, and why that one?
Do you kill your own ideas when the evidence says to?
Can you write a spec an engineer can build from without a meeting?
Do you talk to users directly, or only read summaries of them?
evidenceThatCounts: A shipped feature with the metric before and after
A spec with explicit non-goals
Something you cancelled, and the reasoning that killed it
commonGaps: Feature counting instead of outcome ownership
roles.demandNote: Large, mature market with plenty of competition. Well paid, but generalist PM roles attract hundreds of applicants — the AI and fintech variants are where the scarcity is.

roles.title: Product Operations
roles.reality: Makes the product organisation legible: the tracking plan, the feedback pipeline, the launch checklist, the dashboard everyone actually trusts. Exists because PMs at scale spend half their time re-deriving the same numbers, and someone has to own the plumbing.
screensFor: Can you build a tracking plan a whole org will follow?
Can you turn scattered feedback into a ranked, evidenced list?
Do you know why two dashboards disagree, and how to fix it?
evidenceThatCounts: An instrumentation or tracking plan you designed and shipped
A feedback pipeline that changed what got built
A metric definition you standardised across teams
roles.demandNote: A newer function, growing steadily at companies past roughly 50 people. Often an easier entry into product than a PM role, with much of the same surface area.

roles.title: Strategy & Business Operations
roles.reality: The function a founder or executive hands the problems that do not have an owner: a pricing change, a market entry, a model of whether a segment is worth serving. Analytical work whose output is a decision, not a deck, and increasingly the internal home for 'what does AI change about how we operate'.
screensFor: Can you build a model of a decision and defend its assumptions?
Can you get the data yourself when nobody will build you a dashboard?
Can you write a recommendation an executive can act on in one page?
Do you follow through on execution, or stop at the analysis?
evidenceThatCounts: A model behind a real decision, with the assumptions written down
A pricing, segmentation or market analysis that changed course
SQL or spreadsheet work you did yourself rather than requested
commonGaps: Analysis that never converts into a decision
Cannot get at the data without help
roles.demandNote: Consistently in demand and unusually well paid relative to the experience required. The standard route into general management, and one of the few roles where founder experience reads as directly relevant.

roles.title: Data Engineer
roles.reality: Owns the pipelines and the models underneath everything else — dashboards, ML features, the numbers in the board pack. Judged on whether the data arrives on time, is correct, and can be trusted without being re-checked. AI has made this more valuable, not less: retrieval and evaluation both run on the same plumbing.
screensFor: Can you design a schema that survives changing requirements?
How do you handle late, duplicate and malformed records?
Can you make a pipeline idempotent and backfillable?
Do you test data, or only code?
evidenceThatCounts: A pipeline you built that is still running and still trusted
A data quality incident you found and prevented recurring
dbt, Airflow or equivalent orchestration you actually own
commonGaps: No cost awareness on warehouse spend
roles.demandNote: Demand has stayed high through every hype cycle because every AI project eventually blocks on data access. Less glamorous than model work and significantly easier to get hired into.

roles.title: Machine Learning Engineer
roles.reality: Takes models into production and keeps them there: feature pipelines, training and serving infrastructure, drift monitoring, rollback. Distinct from AI engineering — that builds over someone else's model, this one owns models you train, evaluate and are accountable for.
screensFor: Can you explain train/serve skew and how you detect it?
How do you know a deployed model has degraded?
Can you cost a training run and a serving fleet?
Do you version data as carefully as you version code?
evidenceThatCounts: A model in production with its monitoring and rollback story
An offline/online evaluation gap you diagnosed
Feature pipelines shared between training and serving
roles.demandNote: Among the best paid engineering roles in the market, and genuinely hard to fill — the combination of statistics and production engineering is rare. The bar is high and interview loops are long.

roles.title: Security Engineer
roles.reality: Finds what an attacker would find, and makes the secure path the easy one. Split between review and reaction: threat modelling, code and infrastructure review, and incident response when something lands. AI has added a new surface nobody has fully mapped — prompt injection, agent permissions, data exfiltration through model outputs.
screensFor: Can you threat-model a feature before it is built?
Do you know why a control fails in practice, not just in theory?
Can you run an incident calmly and write the postmortem?
Do you understand the new AI attack surface?
evidenceThatCounts: A vulnerability you found and the fix you shipped
A threat model for a real system
CTF placings, disclosures, or published security research
commonGaps: Policy writing with no engineering depth
Blocks delivery instead of enabling it
roles.demandNote: Persistent shortage, made worse by AI systems shipping faster than anyone can review them. Application security in particular has more open roles than credible candidates.

roles.title: Design Engineer
roles.reality: Sits between design and engineering and ships the interface: design systems, interaction details, prototypes real enough to judge. Valued because the gap between a Figma file and a shipped screen is where most product quality is lost.
screensFor: Can you build a design system others can actually use?
Do you notice a four-pixel misalignment and a missing focus state?
Can you prototype fast enough to settle an argument?
Do you understand accessibility beyond an audit score?
evidenceThatCounts: Interfaces you designed and built, live and linkable
A design system or component library you own
Accessibility work with before and after evidence
commonGaps: Engineering without visual judgement, or the reverse
roles.demandNote: A small field with real scarcity: most engineers cannot design and most designers cannot ship. AI code generation has raised the premium on taste, since generating a passable interface is now trivial and judging one is not.

roles.title: Developer Advocate
roles.reality: Builds the things that make other engineers want to use your platform: demos, documentation, talks, sample applications, and the feedback loop back into product. Half teaching, half engineering, and measured on adoption rather than applause.
screensFor: Can you explain something hard clearly, in writing and on stage?
Do you build real things, or only talk about them?
Can you tie your work to activation or adoption numbers?
evidenceThatCounts: Published writing or talks with an audience
Sample applications and documentation people actually use
An adoption metric you moved
commonGaps: Marketing voice rather than a practitioner's
roles.demandNote: Hiring is cyclical and tied to developer-tool funding, which is currently strong for AI platforms. A strong public body of work matters more here than in any other role on this list.

roles.title: Sales Engineer
roles.reality: The technical half of a sales team: runs the proof of concept, answers the architecture objection, and makes the buyer's engineers believe it will work. Commission-bearing, which puts total compensation well above most engineering bands for people who can carry both sides.
screensFor: Can you demo under pressure and handle a hostile technical question?
Can you scope a proof of concept that closes rather than impresses?
Do you understand the buyer's economics, not just their stack?
evidenceThatCounts: Proofs of concept you ran that converted
Technical objections you turned around
Evidence of building in front of a customer
commonGaps: Demos that impress engineers and close nothing
roles.demandNote: Strongly in demand wherever enterprise AI is being sold, and one of the highest-earning routes available to an engineer who is comfortable with people. Closely adjacent to the FDE path.

roles.title: Engineering Manager
roles.reality: Accountable for a team's output, health and growth. The work is hiring, feedback, unblocking, and holding a technical standard you no longer personally enforce by writing the code. The transition breaks people who measure themselves by what they built this week.
screensFor: Have you hired, and have you managed someone out?
How do you handle an underperformer fairly and quickly?
Can you keep technical judgement without taking the keyboard?
How do you measure a team's health beyond velocity?
evidenceThatCounts: A team you grew, with what happened to the people in it
A delivery turnaround you led
Evidence of mentoring that produced promotions
commonGaps: Senior engineer with a title but no people practice
roles.demandNote: Always in demand, but harder to enter from outside: most companies promote internally. Founder and lead experience is the usual side entrance.

roles.title: Staff / Principal Engineer
roles.reality: Senior technical leadership without direct reports. Picks the problems worth solving, sets technical direction across teams, and is trusted to be right about decisions that are expensive to reverse. Measured in organisational impact, not code volume.
screensFor: Can you name a technical decision you drove and its second-order effects?
Can you write a design document that aligns several teams?
Do you choose problems, or wait to be assigned them?
Can you disagree with a director and keep the relationship?
evidenceThatCounts: A design document that changed how several teams worked
A migration or rewrite you led that landed
Evidence of raising other engineers' output
commonGaps: Deep expertise with no organisational influence
roles.demandNote: The best-paid individual contributor track in software, and deliberately scarce — companies hire few and promote slowly. Requires a track record that is hard to fake.

roles.title: Growth Product Manager
roles.reality: Owns a number — activation, retention or revenue — rather than a surface. Runs a queue of experiments against it, most of which fail, and is judged on the compounding of the ones that do not. Requires comfort with statistics and with being wrong in public.
screensFor: Can you define activation and prove it predicts retention?
Do you know when your sample is too small to call?
Can you build a pricing or onboarding experiment end to end?
Do you report your failed experiments as readily as your wins?
evidenceThatCounts: Experiments with pre-registered metrics, including the failures
A retention or activation curve you moved
A pricing or packaging change you shipped and measured
roles.demandNote: Cooled from its peak but still well paid, and the skills transfer cleanly into general product work. Strongest demand at consumer and product-led-growth companies.

roles.title: Equity Research Analyst
roles.reality: Covers a handful of companies in depth and publishes a view with a number attached. The work is building and defending a model, reading filings closely enough to catch what the summary omits, and speaking to management, customers and competitors until the story either holds or breaks. Being right matters less than being early and being able to show your reasoning.
screensFor: Can you build a three-statement model from a filing, unaided?
Can you defend your assumptions when someone senior attacks them?
Do you read the footnotes, or only the press release?
Can you write a view in one page that a portfolio manager will act on?
evidenceThatCounts: A full initiation note on a real company, with the model behind it
A call you made publicly, including the ones that went wrong
CFA progress, or equivalent demonstrable financial fluency
commonGaps: Modelling mechanics without an actual view
Cannot write concisely enough to be read
No primary research beyond what the company published
roles.demandNote: Sell-side seats have been shrinking for a decade under research-unbundling rules, while buy-side and independent research have held up. Entry is competitive and heavily credential-gated; the work itself is durable.

roles.title: Portfolio Manager
roles.reality: Owns a mandate and is measured against a benchmark, publicly and continuously. Most of the job is position sizing, risk budgeting and deciding what not to own; idea generation is the smaller half. The difficult part is psychological — holding a position through a drawdown, or cutting one you argued for in writing.
screensFor: How do you size a position, and what makes you cut it?
Can you separate a good decision from a good outcome?
Do you understand your mandate's constraints and tracking error?
What is your edge, and why has it not been arbitraged away?
evidenceThatCounts: A track record with the methodology stated, including the bad years
A written investment process you actually followed
Risk work: drawdown control, correlation, position limits
commonGaps: Backtests presented as a track record
Cannot attribute returns to a repeatable process
roles.demandNote: Few seats and slow turnover — this is usually reached from analyst or advisory work rather than hired into. Passive flows have compressed the active universe, but assets under management keep growing in India and Asia.

roles.title: Quantitative Researcher
roles.reality: Turns a market hypothesis into a testable signal and then tries very hard to kill it. The craft is not modelling — it is avoiding self-deception: survivorship bias, look-ahead, overfitting, and transaction costs that quietly eat the edge. Most research ends in a negative result, which is the job working correctly.
screensFor: How do you guard against look-ahead bias and overfitting?
Can you cost a strategy properly — slippage, impact, borrow?
Do you know when your sample is too short to conclude anything?
Can you write code others can rerun and audit?
evidenceThatCounts: A backtest with honest costs and an out-of-sample period
A strategy you abandoned, and the test that killed it
Strong statistics and programming, demonstrably
commonGaps: Machine learning applied without financial intuition
signals: Python or R at research depth
roles.demandNote: Well paid and genuinely hard to enter — funds screen heavily on mathematics and on evidence you can resist fooling yourself. AI skills help, but only alongside real statistical discipline.

roles.title: Venture Capital Associate
roles.reality: Sources deals, runs diligence, and writes the memo a partnership argues over. Most of the week is meeting founders who will not get funded and maintaining the relationships that produce the ones who will. Judgement is only tested on a five-to-ten-year lag, so in the short run you are measured on sourcing, speed and the quality of your written thinking.
screensFor: Can you source proprietary deal flow, not just inbound?
Can you write a memo that reaches a clear recommendation?
Do you understand how a fund actually makes money — and the power law?
Can you diligence a market and a team, not just a product?
evidenceThatCounts: Investment memos on real companies, with your recommendation stated
A founder network you built rather than inherited
Angel investments, scout work, or a syndicate you ran
commonGaps: No sourcing ability — waits for inbound
Cannot say no clearly or quickly
roles.demandNote: Extremely competitive and largely network-gated, with few seats and slow turnover. Operating or founding experience is now the most common way in, which makes it unusually reachable for people who have built something.

roles.title: Investment Banking Analyst
roles.reality: Builds the models and materials behind transactions — mergers, raises, listings — under deadlines set by other people's calendars. The hours are the defining feature and are not exaggerated. What you actually acquire is transaction mechanics, modelling speed and a network, which is why most people treat it as a two-year entry ticket rather than a career.
screensFor: Can you build and audit an LBO or merger model at speed?
Is your work accurate under time pressure and little sleep?
Can you produce client-ready materials without hand-holding?
Do you understand valuation beyond running a comparables screen?
evidenceThatCounts: Modelling tests passed — these are usually the real filter
Transaction exposure, including what your specific contribution was
Valuation work you can walk through line by line
commonGaps: No view on why a deal makes sense
roles.demandNote: Cyclical with deal volume and intensely competitive at entry, with recruiting running years ahead of start dates. Exit options remain the strongest reason people take it.

roles.title: Risk Manager
roles.reality: Quantifies what could go wrong and holds the line when revenue disagrees. The technical half is exposure measurement, stress testing and limits; the harder half is institutional — being the person who says no to a desk that is making money, and being able to evidence why. AI models have added a whole category nobody has fully learned to govern yet.
screensFor: Can you explain the limits of a value-at-risk number?
Can you design a stress test that a business will not dismiss?
Do you hold a limit under pressure from a revenue desk?
Do you understand how a model fails, not only how it scores?
evidenceThatCounts: A risk framework or limit structure you designed
A loss or near-miss you flagged before it happened
FRM, or demonstrable quantitative risk depth
commonGaps: Reporting risk rather than managing it
Cannot translate a number into a decision
roles.demandNote: Steady, regulation-driven demand that holds up through downturns, and model risk around AI systems is a genuinely new and under-supplied specialism.

roles.title: Financial Adviser
roles.reality: Manages other people's money and, more accurately, their behaviour around it. The financial planning is the straightforward part; the value is in stopping someone selling at the bottom, and in asking the questions that surface what the money is actually for. It is a relationship business with a regulatory spine, and it compounds slowly — the book you build in year three pays you in year ten.
screensFor: Can you build trust with someone about the most private thing they own?
Do you know where advice ends and regulated recommendation begins?
Can you explain a drawdown to a frightened client without jargon?
Can you actually bring in clients, or only service them?
evidenceThatCounts: Clients advised and retained, with assets and tenure
Required certification — NISM Series X-A in India, CFP internationally
A written advice process, including how you handle a market fall
roles.demandNote: Structurally growing in India as household savings shift into financial assets, and the adviser population is far too small for the demand. Slow to start, and the economics are excellent once a book exists.

roles.title: Family Office Analyst
roles.reality: Runs the whole balance sheet for one family or a handful of them: public markets, private holdings, real estate, succession, tax and the occasional operating business. The breadth is the appeal and the difficulty — you are expected to have a view on everything, and discretion matters more than brilliance.
screensFor: Can you handle allocation across genuinely illiquid assets?
Do you understand succession, trusts and tax structuring?
Can you be trusted with information that never leaves the room?
Can you evaluate a direct investment without a bank's diligence pack?
evidenceThatCounts: Multi-asset allocation work, including private markets
Direct or co-investment diligence you performed
Evidence of long-tenure, high-trust client relationships
commonGaps: Wrong temperament for a discreet, unhurried setting
roles.demandNote: Quietly expanding as first-generation wealth in India and Asia reaches the stage of needing structure. Roles are rarely advertised and almost always filled through referral.

roles.title: Supply Chain Analyst
roles.reality: Decides how much of what to hold where, and is wrong in two expensive directions — stockouts and dead inventory. The work is forecasting, planning and the negotiation that follows when sales and operations disagree about the same number. AI forecasting has improved the maths and left the organisational argument entirely intact.
screensFor: Can you build a demand forecast and state its error honestly?
Do you understand safety stock and service-level trade-offs?
Can you run an S&OP cycle where functions disagree?
Can you get the data yourself when the ERP will not give it to you?
evidenceThatCounts: A forecast you owned, with accuracy measured over time
An inventory or service-level improvement you can quantify
Strong spreadsheet and SQL work, demonstrably
commonGaps: Reporting the plan rather than owning it
roles.demandNote: Demand rose sharply after the supply shocks of the early 2020s and has stayed elevated as firms carry resilience buffers. Analytical supply-chain people remain harder to find than generalist operations staff.

roles.title: Operations Manager
roles.reality: Owns whether the thing actually happens — throughput, cost per unit, quality, and the people doing the work. Success is unglamorous and cumulative: a process that used to break weekly now breaks monthly. The step up to COO is mostly about whether you can build the system rather than be the system.
screensFor: Can you find the constraint and fix it, rather than optimising everywhere?
Can you run a team through a change they did not want?
Do you measure the process, or only its output?
Can you cost an operation per unit?
evidenceThatCounts: A process you rebuilt with before and after numbers
A team you led through a difficult operational change
Cost or throughput improvements you can quantify
commonGaps: Improvements that decay once you stop watching
roles.demandNote: Broad and durable demand across manufacturing, logistics and fast-growing startups. Underrated as a route to general management, and unusually open to people with founder experience.

roles.title: Procurement Manager
roles.reality: Decides who supplies you and on what terms, then lives with the consequences. Savings are the headline metric and the least interesting part; the real work is supplier risk, dependency and the contract clause that matters only once, when something goes wrong. Cloud and software spend has pulled this function into technology organisations that never had one.
screensFor: Can you run a competitive sourcing process end to end?
Do you evaluate total cost of ownership, not unit price?
Can you negotiate without destroying the supplier relationship?
Do you understand concentration and single-source risk?
evidenceThatCounts: A sourcing exercise you ran, with the savings and the terms
A supplier risk you identified and mitigated
Contract negotiation you led rather than supported
commonGaps: Price focus that ignores total cost
roles.demandNote: Steady, and rising in technology firms specifically, where software and cloud commitments are now among the largest line items and few engineers want to own them.

roles.title: Data Analyst
roles.reality: Answers the questions the business does not yet know how to ask properly. Most of the job is defining the question and the metric before touching any data, then presenting the answer so it actually changes a decision. The technical bar is lower than data engineering; the communication bar is much higher.
screensFor: Can you turn a vague request into a well-specified question?
Is your SQL correct on joins, duplicates and time windows?
Can you present a finding so that someone acts on it?
Do you know when the data cannot answer the question?
evidenceThatCounts: An analysis that changed a decision, with what changed
A dashboard people actually use, and its metric definitions
SQL depth demonstrated on real, messy data
commonGaps: Metric definitions that quietly disagree across teams
Cannot say when a finding is not significant
roles.demandNote: The broadest entry point into data work and the most exposed to AI assistance for routine querying. The durable part of the role is question framing and influence, so lean there.

roles.title: Product Designer
roles.reality: Decides how the product behaves before deciding how it looks. The work is research, flows and states — especially the empty, loading and error ones nobody demos — and then defending those decisions to people who will describe them as personal preference. AI has made producing screens cheap, which has shifted the value firmly onto judgement and research.
screensFor: Can you show the reasoning behind a design, not just the outcome?
Do you design the error and empty states, or only the happy path?
Can you run research and change your mind because of it?
Can you work within an existing system rather than restyling it?
evidenceThatCounts: Case studies showing the problem, the options and why you chose one
Shipped work with a measured outcome
Research that visibly changed the design
commonGaps: Portfolio of polished screens with no reasoning
roles.demandNote: Cooled sharply from the 2021 peak and remains competitive at junior level. Senior designers who can research and argue from evidence are still genuinely scarce.

roles.title: Site Reliability Engineer
roles.reality: Owns whether the system stays up and what it costs to keep it there. The work splits between building the automation that removes toil and being the person who runs the incident at 3am. Error budgets are the distinctive idea: reliability is a number you spend deliberately, not a target you maximise.
screensFor: Can you debug a production system you did not build, under pressure?
Do you understand error budgets and how they change what ships?
Can you automate toil away rather than absorbing it?
Can you write a blameless postmortem people learn from?
evidenceThatCounts: An incident you ran, and the postmortem you wrote
Automation that measurably reduced manual work or downtime
Observability you built — tracing, alerting that is actually actionable
commonGaps: Alerting so noisy it gets ignored
No cost awareness on the infrastructure being run
roles.demandNote: Consistently in demand and well paid, with a bar that has risen as systems have grown more distributed. AI workloads have added GPU capacity and cost management as a genuinely new specialism.

roles.title: Security Analyst
roles.reality: Watches what is happening across the estate and decides what matters. Most alerts are noise, and the skill is triage — knowing which signal is worth waking someone for. It is the most accessible way into security and the most common route to engineering or threat-intelligence work later.
screensFor: Can you triage an alert queue without missing the real one?
Do you know what normal looks like well enough to spot abnormal?
Can you investigate an incident and write it up clearly?
Do you understand the frameworks — MITRE ATT&CK, the kill chain?
evidenceThatCounts: Investigations you ran, and what you concluded
Detection rules you wrote that reduced false positives
Home lab, CTF placings, or Security+ level knowledge shown in practice
commonGaps: Tool operation without understanding the underlying attack
Cannot write an investigation up for a non-technical reader
No scripting, so everything stays manual
roles.demandNote: The most open entry point in security, with persistent staffing shortages in monitoring teams. Routine triage is being automated, so the durable value is in investigation and detection engineering.
